first.rationale: The two measured declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are funnel-internal and compounding: onboarding completion sits upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly recovers part of both numbers, whereas activation messaging (memory_91) only addresses the downstream symptom. That makes simplify_onboarding the highest-leverage single slot for sustainable qualified revenue. I am deliberately not chasing the competitor with promotional_pricing despite memory_73's 'strong acquisition and revenue lift': the summary records acquisition and top-line revenue but says nothing about retention, margin, or LTV of discount-acquired SMBs, and price-led acquisition into a price war is the classic way to book revenue that is not durable or qualified. Hence memory_73 is one of my three verification pulls \u2014 I want to see whether the original record measured downstream value or only signup volume before I permanently rule it out. memory_86 and memory_31 are the two pillars of my intended action and must be checked directly: both are consolidated summaries with no effect sizes, no segment boundaries, and no decay information, and memory_31 is 64 days old, from a pre-competitor market. There is also a specific downstream risk inside my own chosen action: memory_31's mechanism is 'cutting required fields at signup,' which removes exactly the qualification signal used to route and score leads. Uncut, that can lift raw activation while degrading lead quality and pipeline \u2014 volume up, qualified revenue flat or down. It could also cannibalize the demo-request path that memory_44 says wins enterprise. So I will scope the test to self-serve SMB only, leave the enterprise sales-assist path untouched, and instrument on qualified-pipeline and 30/60-day retention rather than completion rate alone. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout: the evidence is real but summarized and the market has changed since it was gathered, so I want a measured read before committing further capacity. If verification shows memory_86 or memory_31 never tracked value past first-week activation, I will downscale to a guarded test and treat the recovered completion rate as unproven rather than banked.

final.rationale:
Verification changed the picture in one decisive way. memory_73's summary ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') omitted the finding that mattered most: exp_73 showed 30-day retention -12% and the original record carries an explicit instruction NOT to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth, because the discounted cohort does not survive first renewal. The +18% qualified revenue was a first-cycle artifact. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is now affirmatively ruled out, not merely deprioritized — and matching the competitor on price would have been the intuitive move precisely because the consolidated summary hid the decay. I am treating this as evidence that consolidated summaries here systematically drop downstream-value terms, which lowers my trust in the two memories I could not pull (memory_91, memory_57, memory_44) by the same amount.

Proceeding with simplify_onboarding, but weighted toward the exp_86 mechanism rather than exp_31's. exp_86 is the cleanest result available: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3% — value moves in the same direction as volume, which is the opposite of the exp_73 pattern. It also targets the two observed declines at their upstream point, since onboarding completion (-4%) gates activation (-6%). exp_31 is confirmed but weaker for this objective: +15% signup and +9% activation converted to only +4% qualified revenue with retention -1%, meaning most of the funnel lift did not become durable value, and the mechanism (cutting required fields) is the one that strips lead-qualification signal. So I will shorten and restructure the onboarding flow rather than aggressively strip signup fields; any field removal is limited to genuinely post-signup steps.

Scoping and guards: self-serve SMB only, since exp_31 explicitly did not replicate on other segments and exp_86's segment breadth is unstated. The enterprise demo-request path stays untouched so the sales-assisted flow is not cannibalized. Primary readout is 30- and 60-day retention and qualified pipeline, not completion rate — completion is the intermediate metric that exp_73 proves can rise while value falls. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout: exp_86 is 24 days old and predates the competitor's entry, so the price-sensitive segment now churning may behave differently, and I want a measured read before committing more capacity. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving this week: whether onboarding improvements retain accounts that are leaving on price rather than on friction. If the retention signal comes back flat, the correct conclusion is that this is a pricing-position problem that discounting still cannot fix, not a reason to revisit exp_73.
